claim: Dietary threonine markedly increased daily sleep amount in Drosophila in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Dietary threonine markedly increased daily sleep amount and decreased the latency to sleep onset in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing dose-dependent effects of dietary threonine on sleep amount in Drosophila, as shown in Figure 1 and related supplementary figures.

claim: Dietary threonine decreased the latency to sleep onset in Drosophila in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Dietary threonine markedly increased daily sleep amount and decreased the latency to sleep onset in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing dose-dependent effects of dietary threonine on sleep latency in Drosophila, as shown in Figure 1 and related supplementary figures.

claim: High levels of synaptic GABA suppressed sleep-promoting effects of dietary threonine (SPET).
source: High levels of synaptic GABA or pharmacological activation of metabotropic GABA receptors (GABAB-R) suppressed SPET.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that genetic or pharmacological elevation of GABA levels suppresses SPET, as shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Pharmacological activation of metabotropic GABA receptors (GABAB-R) suppressed SPET.
source: High levels of synaptic GABA or pharmacological activation of metabotropic GABA receptors (GABAB-R) suppressed SPET.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that SKF-97541, an agonist of metabotropic GABA receptors, suppressed SPET, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Synaptic blockade of GABAergic neurons enhanced sleep drive non-additively with SPET.
source: By contrast, synaptic blockade of GABAergic neurons or transgenic depletion of GABAB-R in the ellipsoid body R2 neurons enhanced sleep drive non-additively with SPET.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that conditional blockade of GABAergic transmission using shibirets promoted sleep and masked SPET, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transgenic depletion of GABAB-R in the ellipsoid body R2 neurons enhanced sleep drive non-additively with SPET.
source: By contrast, synaptic blockade of GABAergic neurons or transgenic depletion of GABAB-R in the ellipsoid body R2 neurons enhanced sleep drive non-additively with SPET.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that RNAi-mediated depletion of GABAB-R2 or GABAB-R3 in R2 EB neurons promoted sleep and masked SPET, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Dietary threonine reduced GABA levels in Drosophila.
source: Dietary threonine reduced GABA levels, weakened metabotropic GABA responses in R2 neurons, and ameliorated memory deficits in plasticity mutants.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that dietary threonine decreased the relative levels of GABA among other amino acids, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Dietary threonine weakened metabotropic GABA responses in R2 neurons.
source: Dietary threonine reduced GABA levels, weakened metabotropic GABA responses in R2 neurons, and ameliorated memory deficits in plasticity mutants.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that dietary threonine dampened the GABA-induced elevation of cAMP levels in R2 EB neurons, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Dietary threonine ameliorated memory deficits in plasticity mutants.
source: Dietary threonine reduced GABA levels, weakened metabotropic GABA responses in R2 neurons, and ameliorated memory deficits in plasticity mutants.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that dietary threonine substantially improved short-term memory in dumb2 mutants and rescued memory deficit in rutabaga mutants, as shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genetic elevation of neuronal threonine levels was sufficient for facilitating sleep onset.
source: Moreover, genetic elevation of neuronal threonine levels was sufficient for facilitating sleep onset.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that loss-of-function mutations in CG5955 (threonine 3-dehydrogenase) elevated endogenous threonine levels and shortened sleep latency, as shown in Figure 7.

claim: Threonine is a physiologically relevant, sleep-promoting molecule that may link neuronal metabolism of amino acids to GABAergic control of sleep drive via the neuronal substrate of sleep homeostasis.
source: Taken together, these data define threonine as a physiologically relevant, sleep-promoting molecule that may intimately link neuronal metabolism of amino acids to GABAergic control of sleep drive via the neuronal substrate of sleep homeostasis.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript, including genetic, pharmacological, and behavioral data.

claim: The circadian clock and sleep homeostasis are two key regulators that shape daily sleep behaviors in animals.
source: The circadian clock and sleep homeostasis are two key regulators that shape daily sleep behaviors in animals (Borbély, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Borbély, 1982, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Sleep behavior is conserved among mammals, insects, and even lower eukaryotes.
source: Sleep behavior is conserved among mammals, insects, and even lower eukaryotes (Allada and Siegel, 2008; Joiner, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Allada and Siegel, 2008 and Joiner, 2016, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: The voltage-gated potassium channel Shaker is a sleep-regulatory gene in Drosophila.
source: Since the identification of the voltage-gated potassium channel Shaker as a sleep-regulatory gene in Drosophila (Cirelli et al., 2005), fruit flies have been one of the most advantageous genetic models to dissect molecular and neural components that are important for sleep homeostasis and plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cirelli et al., 2005.

claim: The inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) has a sleep-promoting role that is conserved in invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: For instance, the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is known to have a sleep-promoting role that is conserved in invertebrates and vertebrates.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge in the field, as indicated by the phrase 'is known to have'.

claim: Hypomorphic mutations in mitochondrial GABA-transaminase (GABA-T) elevate GABA levels and lengthen baseline sleep in flies.
source: Hypomorphic mutations in mitochondrial GABA-transaminase (GABA-T) elevate GABA levels and lengthen baseline sleep in flies (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: The long sleep phenotype in GABA-T mutants accompanies higher sleep consolidation and shorter latency to sleep onset.
source: The long sleep phenotype in GABA-T mutants accompanies higher sleep consolidation and shorter latency to sleep onset, consistent with the observations that pharmacological enhancement of GABAergic transmission facilitates sleep in flies and mammals, including humans (Holmes and Sugden, 1975; Lancel et al., 1998; Schneider et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Holmes and Sugden, 1975; Lancel et al., 1998; Schneider et al., 1977.

claim: Pharmacological enhancement of GABAergic transmission facilitates sleep in flies and mammals, including humans.
source: The long sleep phenotype in GABA-T mutants accompanies higher sleep consolidation and shorter latency to sleep onset, consistent with the observations that pharmacological enhancement of GABAergic transmission facilitates sleep in flies and mammals, including humans (Holmes and Sugden, 1975; Lancel et al., 1998; Schneider et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Holmes and Sugden, 1975; Lancel et al., 1998; Schneider et al., 1977.

claim: Resistance to dieldrin (Rdl), a Drosophila homolog of the ionotropic GABA receptor, suppresses wake-promoting circadian pacemaker neurons in adult flies to exert sleep-promoting effects.
source: In addition, resistance to dieldrin (Rdl), a Drosophila homolog of the ionotropic GABA receptor, suppresses wake-promoting circadian pacemaker neurons in adult flies to exert sleep-promoting effects (Agosto et al., 2008; Chung et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2014a; Parisky et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Agosto et al., 2008; Chung et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2014a; Parisky et al., 2008.

claim: 4,5,6,7-tetrahydroisoxazolo[5,4 c]pyridin-3-ol (THIP), an agonist of the ionotropic GABA receptor, promotes sleep in insects and mammals.
source: Similarly, 4,5,6,7-tetrahydroisoxazolo[5,4 c]pyridin-3-ol (THIP), an agonist of the ionotropic GABA receptor, promotes sleep in insects and mammals (Dissel et al., 2015; Faulhaber et al., 1997; Lancel, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dissel et al., 2015; Faulhaber et al., 1997; Lancel, 1997.

claim: Many sleep medications modulate GABAergic transmission.
source: Many sleep medications modulate GABAergic transmission.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field of sleep medicine.

claim: A prominent side effect of anti-epileptic drugs relevant to GABA is causing drowsiness.
source: A prominent side effect of anti-epileptic drugs relevant to GABA is causing drowsiness (Jain and Glauser, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jain and Glauser, 2014.

claim: Glycine supplements improve sleep quality in a way distinct from traditional hypnotic drugs, minimizing deleterious cognitive problems or addiction.
source: Conversely, glycine supplements improve sleep quality in a way distinct from traditional hypnotic drugs, minimizing deleterious cognitive problems or addiction (Bannai and Kawai, 2012; Yamadera et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bannai and Kawai, 2012; Yamadera et al., 2007.

claim: Glycine or D-serine acts as a co-agonist of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) and promotes sleep through the sub-type of ionotropic glutamate receptors.
source: In fact, glycine or D-serine acts as a co-agonist of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) and promotes sleep through the sub-type of ionotropic glutamate receptors (Dai et al., 2019; Kawai et al., 2015; Tomita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dai et al., 2019; Kawai et al., 2015; Tomita et al., 2015.

claim: Emerging evidence supports the roles of amino acid transporters and metabolic enzymes in sleep regulation.
source: Emerging evidence further supports the roles of amino acid transporters and metabolic enzymes in sleep regulation (Aboudhiaf et al., 2018; Sonn et al., 2018; Stahl et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aboudhiaf et al., 2018; Sonn et al., 2018; Stahl et al., 2018.

claim: Starvation induces the expression of metabolic enzymes for serine biosynthesis in Drosophila brains, and elevates free serine levels to suppress sleep via cholinergic signaling.
source: In particular, we have demonstrated that starvation induces the expression of metabolic enzymes for serine biosynthesis in Drosophila brains, and elevates free serine levels to suppress sleep via cholinergic signaling (Sonn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sonn et al., 2018, which represents prior work by the authors.

claim: Cysteine supplementation had the strongest impact on sleep quantity and quality among amino acids tested.
source: The strongest impact on sleep quantity and quality was observed with cysteine supplementation (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing effects of cysteine supplementation on sleep, as shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dietary cysteine compromised locomotion and caused high lethality during sleep assays.
source: However, dietary cysteine compromised locomotion and caused high lethality during our sleep assay (see Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing negative effects of cysteine supplementation, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Threonine supplementation potently elevated total sleep amount by increasing the number of sleep bouts.
source: Intriguingly, threonine supplementation potently elevated total sleep amount by increasing the number of sleep bouts (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that threonine supplementation increased sleep amount and the number of sleep bouts, as shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dietary threonine evidently shortened the latency to sleep onset after lights-off.
source: In addition, dietary threonine evidently shortened the latency to sleep onset after lights-off.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that dietary threonine shortened sleep latency, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The sleep-promoting effects of dietary threonine (SPET) were observed in both male and female flies.
source: The sleep-promoting effects of dietary threonine (SPET) were dose-dependent and observed in both male and female flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing SPET in both male and female flies, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Transgenic silencing of sensory neurons that express gustatory receptors (Gr66a, Gr33a, and Gr5a) or olfactory co-receptor negligibly affected SPET.
source: Transgenic silencing of sensory neurons that express either gustatory receptors (Gr66a, Gr33a, and Gr5a) or olfactory co-receptor (Lone et al., 2016) negligibly affected SPET as compared to relevant heterozygous controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that silencing of sensory neurons did not significantly affect SPET, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Sensory perception of dietary threonine is less likely responsible for SPET.
source: These results suggest that sensory perception of dietary threonine is less likely responsible for SPET.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that silencing of sensory neurons did not significantly affect SPET.

claim: Flies fed nutrient-rich food containing additional protein sources exhibited SPET, although higher concentrations of threonine were required.
source: We further found that flies fed nutrient-rich food containing additional protein sources (e.g., cornmeal, yeast) also exhibited SPET, although higher concentrations of threonine were required (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing SPET on nutrient-rich food, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Flies may ingest smaller volume of daily food on nutrient-rich diet than on sucrose-only diet as a compensation for their difference in calories per volume.
source: We reason that flies may ingest smaller volume of daily food on nutrient-rich diet than on sucrose-only diet as a compensation for their difference in calories per volume (Carvalho et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to Carvalho et al., 2005.

claim: SPET is not limited to carbohydrate-only diets.
source: Nonetheless, these data indicate that SPET is not limited to carbohydrate-only diets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing SPET on nutrient-rich food.

claim: Control- and threonine-fed flies displayed no significant differences in the percentage of flies aroused by a given range of mechanical stimuli in the middle of night.
source: Control- and threonine-fed flies displayed no significant differences in the percentage of flies aroused by a given range of mechanical stimuli in the middle of night (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing no significant difference in arousal threshold, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Threonine-fed flies displayed shorter latency to the first post-stimulus bout of sleep.
source: However, threonine-fed flies displayed shorter latency to the first post-stimulus bout of sleep.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing shorter sleep latency after arousal in threonine-fed flies, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A higher sleep drive, but not a change in sleep depth, may contribute to SPET.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that a higher sleep drive, but not a change in sleep depth, may contribute to SPET.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no change in arousal threshold but shorter sleep latency after arousal.

claim: Rdl and wide awake (wake) are two evolutionarily conserved genes that contribute to circadian clock-dependent control of sleep onset in Drosophila.
source: Rdl and wide awake (wake) are two evolutionarily conserved genes that contribute to circadian clock-dependent control of sleep onset in Drosophila (Agosto et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Agosto et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014a.

claim: A circadian transcription factor, CLOCK (CLK), drives daily rhythmic transcription of wake, particularly in a subset of clock neurons that express the circadian neuropeptide PIGMENT-DISPERSING FACTOR (PDF).
source: A circadian transcription factor, CLOCK (CLK), drives daily rhythmic transcription of wake, particularly in a subset of clock neurons that express the circadian neuropeptide PIGMENT-DISPERSING FACTOR (PDF) (Liu et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2014a.

claim: WAKE acts as a clock output molecule that interacts with RDL, silences the wake-promoting PDF neurons, and facilitates sleep onset.
source: Subsequently, WAKE acts as a clock output molecule that interacts with RDL, silences the wake-promoting PDF neurons, and facilitates sleep onset.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge based on prior research, as indicated by the context.

claim: Female mutants trans-heterozygous for hypomorphic Rdl alleles had shorter sleep latency in control-fed condition than their heterozygous controls.
source: We first confirmed that female mutants trans-heterozygous for hypomorphic Rdl alleles had shorter sleep latency in control-fed condition than their heterozygous controls (Agosto et al., 2008) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data confirming prior findings, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and cites Agosto et al., 2008.

claim: Dietary threonine shortened sleep latency additively with the loss of Rdl function.
source: Dietary threonine, however, shortened sleep latency additively with the loss of Rdl function (p=0.084, by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing additive effects of dietary threonine and Rdl mutation on sleep latency, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trans-heterozygous Rdl mutation did not compromise SPET on daily sleep amount compared to either heterozygous controls.
source: In addition, trans-heterozygous Rdl mutation did not compromise SPET on daily sleep amount compared to either heterozygous controls.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing comparable SPET in Rdl mutants and controls, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Clk function caused long sleep latency in fed condition.
source: We next examined if SPET was suppressed in arrhythmic clock mutants. Loss of Clk function caused long sleep latency in fed condition (Liu et al., 2014a), and SPET had additive effects on the latency phenotype in Clk mutants (Figure 2A, p=0.14 by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2014a and experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SPET had additive effects on the sleep latency phenotype in Clk mutants.
source: We next examined if SPET was suppressed in arrhythmic clock mutants. Loss of Clk function caused long sleep latency in fed condition (Liu et al., 2014a), and SPET had additive effects on the latency phenotype in Clk mutants (Figure 2A, p=0.14 by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing additive effects of SPET in Clk mutants, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Short sleep latency in per mutants likely caused a floor effect, leading to no significant SPET on their sleep latency.
source: On the other hand, short sleep latency in per mutants (Liu et al., 2014a) likely caused a floor effect, leading to no significant SPET on their sleep latency (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and prior knowledge cited from Liu et al., 2014a.

claim: Wild-type and both clock mutants (Clk and per) showed comparable SPET on daily sleep amount.
source: Nonetheless, wild-type and both clock mutants showed comparable SPET on daily sleep amount (Figure 2A, p=0.8367 for Clk mutants; p=0.2573 for per mutants by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing comparable SPET on sleep amount in wild-type and clock mutants, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Overexpression of dominant-negative CLK proteins (CLKDN) in PDF neurons is sufficient to abolish free-running circadian locomotor rhythms.
source: Finally, it has been shown that overexpression of dominant-negative CLK proteins (CLKDN) in PDF neurons is sufficient to abolish free-running circadian locomotor rhythms (Tanoue et al., 2004) and lengthen sleep latency (Liu et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tanoue et al., 2004 and Liu et al., 2014a.

claim: Overexpression of dominant-negative CLK proteins (CLKDN) in PDF neurons lengthens sleep latency.
source: Finally, it has been shown that overexpression of dominant-negative CLK proteins (CLKDN) in PDF neurons is sufficient to abolish free-running circadian locomotor rhythms (Tanoue et al., 2004) and lengthen sleep latency (Liu et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2014a.

claim: CLKDN overexpression in PDF neurons did not suppress SPET.
source: We observed consistent effects of CLKDN overexpression in PDF neurons on sleep drive in control-fed condition, but it did not suppress SPET (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that CLKDN overexpression in PDF neurons did not suppress SPET, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SPET does not require clock-dependent control of sleep onset by circadian clock genes or PDF neurons.
source: These lines of our genetic evidence suggest that SPET does not require clock-dependent control of sleep onset by circadian clock genes or PDF neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that clock mutations and PDF neuron manipulations did not suppress SPET.

claim: Constant dark (DD) following LD entrainment eliminates masking behaviors in direct response to the light transitions while allowing free-running circadian rhythms by endogenous clocks.
source: Constant dark (DD) following LD entrainment eliminates masking behaviors in direct response to the light transitions while allowing free-running circadian rhythms by endogenous clocks (Allada and Chung, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Allada and Chung, 2010, representing established knowledge.

claim: DD did not suppress SPET but rather exaggerated it particularly in male flies.
source: We found that DD did not suppress SPET but rather exaggerated it particularly in male flies (Figure 2C and D, p<0.0001 to SPET on sleep amount or sleep latency in LD by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing enhanced SPET in DD, as shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: SPET was evident even in the absence of light.
source: SPET was thus evident even in the absence of light.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing SPET in DD conditions.

claim: Constant light (LL) abolishes circadian rhythms in wild-type flies.
source: By contrast, constant light (LL) abolishes circadian rhythms in wild-type flies (Emery et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Emery et al., 2000, representing established knowledge.

claim: Control-fed flies completely lost their daily rhythms in sleep-wake cycles in LL.
source: Consequently, control-fed flies completely lost their daily rhythms in sleep-wake cycles (Figure 2C and D) and dampened their sleep latency in LL (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing loss of sleep-wake rhythms in LL, as shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Control-fed flies dampened their sleep latency in LL.
source: Consequently, control-fed flies completely lost their daily rhythms in sleep-wake cycles (Figure 2C and D) and dampened their sleep latency in LL (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing dampened sleep latency in LL, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dietary threonine had significant effects on sleep latency in LL when compared among different time-points.
source: Nonetheless, we observed significant effects of dietary threonine on sleep latency (i.e., shorter sleep latency in threonine-fed flies) when SPET on sleep latency was compared among different time-points in LL (p=0.0003 to control-fed male in LL; p<0.0001 to control-fed female in LL by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing significant effects of dietary threonine on sleep latency in LL, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dietary threonine increased daily sleep amount in LL.
source: Dietary threonine also increased daily sleep amount in LL (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing increased sleep amount in LL, as shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Male flies displayed comparable SPET on daily sleep amount in LD and LL.
source: In fact, male flies displayed comparable SPET on daily sleep amount in LD and LL (p=0.1835 by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing comparable SPET on sleep amount in LD and LL for male flies.

claim: Higher sleep drive by SPET likely operates in a manner independent of circadian clocks and their control of sleep onset.
source: Collectively, these data support that higher sleep drive by SPET likely operates in a manner independent of circadian clocks and their control of sleep onset.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing SPET in various light-dark conditions and clock mutants.

claim: SPET was potently suppressed in GABA-T mutants trans-heterozygous for a null allele (GABA-TPL) over chromosomal deficiency.
source: Interestingly, SPET was potently suppressed in GABA-T mutants trans-heterozygous for a null allele (GABA-TPL) over chromosomal deficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing suppression of SPET in GABA-T mutants, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sensitivity to SPET in GABA-T mutants was partially but significantly rescued by transgenic overexpression of wild-type GABA-T.
source: Their sensitivity to SPET was partially but significantly rescued by transgenic overexpression of wild-type GABA-T (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing rescue of SPET sensitivity by GABA-T overexpression, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and cites Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Trans-heterozygosity of strong GABA-T alleles promoted sleep in control-fed condition.
source: However, the trans-heterozygosity of these strong GABA-T alleles promoted sleep in control-fed condition (Chen et al., 2015), raising the possibility that a ceiling effect may mask SPET.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: GABA-T mutants trans-heterozygous for null over hypomorphic alleles (GABA-TF or GABA-TLL) did not significantly affect baseline sleep in control-fed condition as compared to their heterozygous controls.
source: GABA-T mutants trans-heterozygous for null over hypomorphic alleles (GABA-TF or GABA-TLL) (Chen et al., 2015) did not significantly affect baseline sleep in control-fed condition as compared to their heterozygous controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing no significant effect on baseline sleep in weaker GABA-T mutants, as shown in Figure 3A, and cites Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Weaker GABA-T mutants (trans-heterozygous for null over hypomorphic alleles) still exhibited resistance to SPET.
source: Nonetheless, these mutants still exhibited the resistance to SPET (p<0.0001 to SPET on sleep amount or sleep latency in heterozygous controls by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing resistance to SPET in weaker GABA-T mutants, as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: EOS supplement did not significantly increase daily sleep amount at a given dose in the sleep assay, but it modestly shortened sleep latency in wild-type flies fed control food.
source: EOS supplement did not significantly increase daily sleep amount at a given dose in our sleep assay, but it modestly shortened sleep latency in wild-type flies fed control food (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing effects of EOS on sleep, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SPET was suppressed in EOS-fed flies similarly as in GABA-T mutants.
source: However, SPET was suppressed in EOS-fed flies (p<0.0001 to SPET on sleep amount or sleep latency in control flies by two-way ANOVA) similarly as in GABA-T mutants.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing suppression of SPET by EOS, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GABA-T is a mitochondrial enzyme which metabolizes GABA into succinic semialdehyde.
source: Considering that GABA-T is a mitochondrial enzyme which metabolizes GABA into succinic semialdehyde (Chen et al., 2015), we hypothesized that high GABA levels at GABAergic synapses might interfere with sleep drive by dietary threonine.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Nipecotic acid (NipA) blocks GABA reuptake from synaptic clefts.
source: This idea was further supported by our observation that nipecotic acid (NipA), which blocks GABA reuptake from synaptic clefts (Leal and Neckameyer, 2002), comparably suppressed SPET (Figure 3B, p<0.0001 to SPET on sleep amount or sleep latency in control flies by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leal and Neckameyer, 2002.

claim: Nipecotic acid (NipA) comparably suppressed SPET.
source: This idea was further supported by our observation that nipecotic acid (NipA), which blocks GABA reuptake from synaptic clefts (Leal and Neckameyer, 2002), comparably suppressed SPET (Figure 3B, p<0.0001 to SPET on sleep amount or sleep latency in control flies by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing suppression of SPET by NipA, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SPET may involve a sleep drive relevant to GABA.
source: Collectively, these genetic and pharmacological data suggest that SPET may involve a sleep drive relevant to GABA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that genetic and pharmacological elevation of GABA levels suppresses SPET.

claim: Evidence from adult-specific manipulations of GABA levels excludes possible developmental effects of GABA-T mutation or GABA on SPET.
source: In addition, evidence from our adult-specific manipulations of GABA levels excludes possible developmental effects of GABA-T mutation or GABA on SPET.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design using adult-specific manipulations.

claim: Genetic deficit in the metabolic conversion of GABA to glutamate leads to high levels of GABA in GABA-T mutants while they have low levels of glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate.
source: Genetic deficit in the metabolic conversion of GABA to glutamate leads to high levels of GABA in GABA-T mutants while they have low levels of glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate, a glutamate derivative that enters tricarboxylic cycle (Maguire et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maguire et al., 2015.

claim: Changes in GABA-derived metabolites in GABA-T mutants are accompanied with impairment in energy homeostasis as supported by the high ratio of NAD+/NADH levels and low ATP levels.
source: These changes in GABA-derived metabolites are accompanied with impairment in energy homeostasis as supported by the high ratio of NAD+/NADH levels and low ATP levels in GABA-T mutants.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge based on prior research on GABA-T mutants.

claim: GABA-T mutants cannot survive on carbohydrate-based food (i.e., 5% sucrose +1.5% agar) but their metabolic stress phenotypes are rescued by the supplement of glutamate and other amino acids that can be metabolized to glutamate.
source: Consequently, GABA-T mutants cannot survive on carbohydrate-based food (i.e., 5% sucrose +1.5% agar) but their metabolic stress phenotypes are rescued by the supplement of glutamate and other amino acids that can be metabolized to glutamate.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge based on prior research on GABA-T mutants.

claim: Dietary threonine did not significantly affect ATP levels or the ratio of NAD+/NADH levels.
source: Dietary threonine did not significantly affect ATP levels or the ratio of NAD+/NADH levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing no significant effect of dietary threonine on ATP or NAD+/NADH levels, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pyruvate levels were selectively elevated in threonine-fed flies.
source: However, pyruvate levels were selectively elevated in threonine-fed flies (p<0.0001 to succinate by one-way ANOVA, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test), possibly due to the metabolism of dietary threonine into pyruvate via L-2-amino-acetoacetate (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing elevated pyruvate levels in threonine-fed flies, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and provides a metabolic pathway diagram in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dietary pyruvate itself did not promote sleep.
source: Nonetheless, dietary pyruvate itself did not promote sleep (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing no sleep-promoting effect of dietary pyruvate, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Dietary threonine reduced the relative levels of proline, histidine, alanine, glutamate, and GABA among other amino acids.
source: Quantification of free amino acids further revealed that dietary threonine reduced the relative levels of proline, histidine, alanine, glutamate, and GABA among other amino acids (Figure 4A, p<0.05 or p<0.001 to arginine by one-way ANOVA, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing reduced levels of select amino acids in threonine-fed flies, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Glutamate acts as either a wake- or sleep-promoting neurotransmitter in Drosophila.
source: Since it has been shown that glutamate acts as either a wake- or sleep-promoting neurotransmitter in Drosophila (Guo et al., 2016; Robinson et al., 2016; Tomita et al., 2015; Zimmerman et al., 2017), we asked if co-administration of threonine and glutamate could suppress SPET.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2016; Robinson et al., 2016; Tomita et al., 2015; Zimmerman et al., 2017.

claim: Glutamate supplement negligibly affected SPET.
source: Glutamate supplement, however, negligibly affected SPET (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, p=0.91 for sleep amount; p=0.516 for sleep latency by two-way ANOVA), suggesting that dietary threonine may not limit glutamate levels to promote sleep.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing no significant effect of glutamate supplement on SPET, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dietary threonine may not limit glutamate levels to promote sleep.
source: Glutamate supplement, however, negligibly affected SPET (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, p=0.91 for sleep amount; p=0.516 for sleep latency by two-way ANOVA), suggesting that dietary threonine may not limit glutamate levels to promote sleep.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no effect of glutamate supplement on SPET.

claim: Glutamate supplement can rescue metabolic stress, but not sleep phenotypes, in GABA-T mutants, indicating independent regulatory pathways of GABA-relevant metabolism and sleep.
source: It is noteworthy that glutamate supplement can rescue metabolic stress, but not sleep phenotypes, in GABA-T mutants, indicating independent regulatory pathways of GABA-relevant metabolism and sleep (Maguire et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maguire et al., 2015.

claim: Threonine, but not arginine, induced the CaLexA signal in a subset of GABAergic neurons adjacent to the antennal lobe (LN, lateral neurons).
source: Interestingly, threonine, but not arginine, induced the CaLexA signal in a subset of GABAergic neurons adjacent to the antennal lobe (LN, lateral neurons) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing threonine-induced CaLexA signal in LN, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B and C.

claim: No detectable changes were observed in the CaLexA signals from other sleep-regulatory loci such as mushroom body or dopaminergic neurons upon threonine diet.
source: By contrast, no detectable changes were observed in the CaLexA signals from other sleep-regulatory loci such as mushroom body or dopaminergic neurons upon threonine diet (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D and E).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing no change in CaLexA signals in mushroom body or dopaminergic neurons, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4D and E.

claim: The conditional blockade of synaptic transmission in GABAergic neurons induced sleep in control-fed condition.
source: The conditional blockade of synaptic transmission in GABAergic neurons induced sleep in control-fed condition (Figure 4B), and it significantly masked SPET (p<0.0001 for sleep amount; p=0.0012 for sleep latency by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that shibirets expression in GABAergic neurons induced sleep, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The conditional blockade of synaptic transmission in GABAergic neurons significantly masked SPET.
source: The conditional blockade of synaptic transmission in GABAergic neurons induced sleep in control-fed condition (Figure 4B), and it significantly masked SPET (p<0.0001 for sleep amount; p=0.0012 for sleep latency by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that shibirets expression in GABAergic neurons masked SPET, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Pan-neuronal depletion of metabotropic GABA receptor R1 or R3 (GABAB-R1 or GABAB-R3) partially but consistently induced long sleep phenotypes.
source: These long sleep phenotypes were partially but consistently observed by the pan-neuronal depletion of metabotropic GABA receptor R1 or R3 (GABAB-R1 or GABAB-R3) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing long sleep phenotypes by pan-neuronal depletion of GABAB-R1 or GABAB-R3, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Co-administration of an agonist of metabotropic GABA receptors (SKF-97541), but not of ionotropic GABA receptors (THIP), with threonine suppressed SPET particularly on sleep latency.
source: We further found that co-administration of an agonist of metabotropic GABA receptors (SKF-97541), but not of ionotropic GABA receptors (THIP), with threonine suppressed SPET particularly on sleep latency (Figure 4D, p=0.1285 for THIP; p=0.0096 for SKF-97541 by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that SKF-97541, but not THIP, suppressed SPET on sleep latency, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A previous study mapped a subset of ellipsoid body (EB) neurons in the adult fly brain (R2 EB neurons) as a neural locus important for sleep homeostasis.
source: A previous study mapped a subset of ellipsoid body (EB) neurons in the adult fly brain (hereafter referred to as R2 EB neurons) as a neural locus important for sleep homeostasis (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Neural activity in R2 EB neurons positively correlates to sleep need.
source: Neural activity in R2 EB neurons positively correlates to sleep need, and the transgenic excitation of R2 EB neurons is sufficient to induce rebound sleep.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge based on prior research, as indicated by the context.

claim: The transgenic excitation of R2 EB neurons is sufficient to induce rebound sleep.
source: Neural activity in R2 EB neurons positively correlates to sleep need, and the transgenic excitation of R2 EB neurons is sufficient to induce rebound sleep.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge based on prior research, as indicated by the context.

claim: The intracellular signaling downstream of metabotropic GABA receptors triggers cAMP synthesis.
source: Since the intracellular signaling downstream of metabotropic GABA receptors triggers cAMP synthesis (Onali et al., 2003), we employed Epac1-camps, a transgenic fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) sensor for cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) (Shafer et al., 2008) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Onali et al., 2003.

claim: Live-brain imaging of the Epac1-camps in R2 EB neurons detected a dose-dependent increase in cAMP levels by a bath application of GABA.
source: Our live-brain imaging of the Epac1-camps in R2 EB neurons detected a dose-dependent increase in cAMP levels by a bath application of GABA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing dose-dependent increase in cAMP levels by GABA, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pre-incubation with tetrodotoxin did not affect the GABA-induced elevation of cAMP levels, indicating cell-autonomous effects of GABA on R2 EB neurons.
source: Pre-incubation with tetrodotoxin did not affect the GABA-induced elevation of cAMP levels, indicating cell-autonomous effects of GABA on these R2 EB neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that tetrodotoxin did not affect GABA-induced cAMP elevation, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Dietary threonine modestly, but significantly, dampened the GABA response in R2 EB neurons.
source: We further found that dietary threonine modestly, but significantly, dampened the GABA response in R2 EB neurons (Figure 5B), validating that dietary threonine modulates the neural activity of this homeostatic sleep driver.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing dampened GABA response in R2 EB neurons of threonine-fed flies, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The RNAi-mediated depletion of GABAB-R2 or GABAB-R3 in R2 EB neurons modestly promoted sleep in control-fed conditions.
source: The RNAi-mediated depletion of GABAB-R2 or GABAB-R3 in R2 EB neurons modestly promoted sleep in control-fed conditions (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing modest sleep promotion by GABAB-R2 or GABAB-R3 depletion in R2 EB neurons, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The RNAi-mediated depletion of GABAB-R2 or GABAB-R3 in R2 EB neurons significantly masked SPET on sleep amount and on sleep latency.
source: Moreover, it significantly masked SPET on sleep amount (p=0.0093 for GABAB-R2; p=0.0007 for GABAB-R3 by two-way ANOVA) and on sleep latency (p=0.0072 for GABAB-R2; p<0.0001 for GABAB-R3 by two-way ANOVA), as compared to heterozygous controls.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that GABAB-R2 or GABAB-R3 depletion in R2 EB neurons masked SPET, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Genetic suppression of the metabotropic GABA transmission in R2 EB neurons phenotypically mimics SPET at the levels of neural activity (i.e., weaker GABA responses) and sleep behaviors (i.e., higher sleep drive).
source: Nonetheless, these results indicate that genetic suppression of the metabotropic GABA transmission in R2 EB neurons phenotypically mimics SPET at the levels of neural activity (i.e., weaker GABA responses) and sleep behaviors (i.e., higher sleep drive).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that GABAB-R depletion in R2 EB neurons produces similar effects to SPET.

claim: Sleep deprivation impairs learning in Drosophila.
source: Sleep deprivation impairs learning in Drosophila (Seugnet et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Seugnet et al., 2008.

claim: Genetic or pharmacological induction of sleep ameliorates memory deficits in plasticity mutants.
source: By contrast, genetic or pharmacological induction of sleep ameliorates memory deficits in plasticity mutants (Dissel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dissel et al., 2015.

claim: Hypomorphic mutants of D1-like dopamine receptor 1 (dumb2) displayed impairment in short-term memory (STM).
source: Hypomorphic mutants of D1-like dopamine receptor 1 (dumb2) displayed impairment in STM (Figure 6B), consistent with previous observation (Seugnet et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing STM impairment in dumb2 mutants, as shown in Figure 6B, and cites Seugnet et al., 2008.

claim: Dietary threonine substantially improved STM in dumb mutants.
source: Dietary threonine substantially improved STM in dumb mutants (Figure 6B), and comparably rescued memory deficit in plasticity mutants of rutabaga, a Drosophila homolog of adenylate cyclase (Dissel et al., 2015) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing STM improvement in dumb mutants by dietary threonine, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Dietary threonine comparably rescued memory deficit in plasticity mutants of rutabaga, a Drosophila homolog of adenylate cyclase.
source: Dietary threonine substantially improved STM in dumb mutants (Figure 6B), and comparably rescued memory deficit in plasticity mutants of rutabaga, a Drosophila homolog of adenylate cyclase (Dissel et al., 2015) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing memory rescue in rutabaga mutants by dietary threonine, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and cites Dissel et al., 2015.

claim: SPET and caffeine-induced arousal displayed additive effects on daily sleep amount in control flies.
source: SPET and caffeine-induced arousal displayed additive effects on daily sleep amount in control flies (Figure 6C, p=0.5963 by two-way ANOVA) while negligibly affecting their performance index in the memory test (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing additive effects of SPET and caffeine on sleep amount, as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SPET and caffeine-induced arousal negligibly affected the performance index in the memory test in control flies.
source: SPET and caffeine-induced arousal displayed additive effects on daily sleep amount in control flies (Figure 6C, p=0.5963 by two-way ANOVA) while negligibly affecting their performance index in the memory test (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing no significant effect on memory performance in control flies, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Baseline sleep in dumb mutants were relatively insensitive to caffeine.
source: Consistent with the implication of dopaminergic activation in caffeine-induced arousal (Andretic et al., 2008; Nall et al., 2016), baseline sleep in dumb mutants were relatively insensitive to caffeine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and citations to Andretic et al., 2008; Nall et al., 2016.

claim: Co-administration of caffeine and threonine suppressed dumb mutant sleep more evidently than caffeine alone.
source: Co-administration of caffeine and threonine, however, suppressed dumb mutant sleep more evidently than caffeine alone (Figure 6B), and blocked the improvement of their memory deficit by dietary threonine (Figure 6C, p=0.0435 by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing enhanced sleep suppression by co-administration of caffeine and threonine in dumb mutants, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Co-administration of caffeine and threonine blocked the improvement of memory deficit by dietary threonine in dumb mutants.
source: Co-administration of caffeine and threonine, however, suppressed dumb mutant sleep more evidently than caffeine alone (Figure 6B), and blocked the improvement of their memory deficit by dietary threonine (Figure 6C, p=0.0435 by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that caffeine blocked memory improvement by threonine in dumb mutants, as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CG5955 is a fly homolog of threonine 3-dehydrogenase that converts threonine and NAD+ into L-2-amino-acetoacetate, NADH, and H+.
source: CG5955 is a fly homolog of threonine 3-dehydrogenase that converts threonine and NAD+ into L-2-amino-acetoacetate, NADH, and H+ (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of enzyme function and is illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: A transposable P-element insertion in the proximal promoter region of the CG5955 locus reduced the relative levels of CG5955 mRNA.
source: We identified a transposable P-element insertion in the proximal promoter region of the CG5955 locus that reduced the relative levels of CG5955 mRNA (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing reduced CG5955 mRNA levels in the mutant, as shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: CG5955 mutants trans-heterozygous for the hypomorphic allele over chromosomal deficiency displayed a higher ratio of threonine to total protein levels than heterozygous controls.
source: Biochemical analyses of fly extracts confirmed that CG5955 mutants trans-heterozygous for the hypomorphic allele over chromosomal deficiency displayed a higher ratio of threonine to total protein levels than heterozygous controls (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing elevated threonine levels in CG5955 mutants, as shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Either homozygous or trans-heterozygous mutation in CG5955 increased daily sleep amounts compared to heterozygous controls.
source: Behavioral analyses revealed that either homozygous or trans-heterozygous mutation in CG5955 increased daily sleep amounts compared to heterozygous controls (Figure 7D).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing increased sleep in CG5955 mutants, as shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The latency to sleep onset after lights-off was strongly shortened in CG5955 mutants, indicating a high sleep drive.
source: Moreover, the latency to sleep onset after lights-off was strongly shortened in CG5955 mutants, indicating a high sleep drive.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing shortened sleep latency in CG5955 mutants, as shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Pan-neuronal depletion of CG5955 expression was sufficient to mimic CG5955 mutants in terms of their sleep latency phenotype.
source: We further found that pan-neuronal depletion of CG5955 expression was sufficient to mimic CG5955 mutants in terms of their sleep latency phenotype (Figure 7E).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing shortened sleep latency by pan-neuronal CG5955 RNAi, as shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Threonine metabolism in the brain modulates sleep drive in flies.
source: Nonetheless, our genetic, biochemical, and behavioral evidence supports that threonine metabolism in the brain modulates sleep drive in flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental evidence from CG5955 mutant studies.

claim: SPET operates via the down-regulation of metabotropic GABA transmission in R2 EB neurons, a neural locus for generating homeostatic sleep drive.
source: We further elucidate that SPET operates likely via the down-regulation of metabotropic GABA transmission in R2 EB neurons, a neural locus for generating homeostatic sleep drive (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that dietary threonine dampens GABA responses in R2 EB neurons and that GABAB-R depletion in these neurons mimics SPET, with citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Both food availability and nutritional quality substantially affect sleep behaviors in Drosophila.
source: Both food availability and nutritional quality substantially affect sleep behaviors in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Sucrose contents in food and their gustatory perception dominate over dietary protein to affect daily sleep.
source: Sucrose contents in food and their gustatory perception dominate over dietary protein to affect daily sleep (Catterson et al., 2010; Linford et al., 2012; Linford et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Catterson et al., 2010; Linford et al., 2012; Linford et al., 2015.

claim: Starvation promotes arousal in a manner dependent on the circadian clock genes Clock and cycle.
source: Starvation promotes arousal in a manner dependent on the circadian clock genes Clock and cycle (Keene et al., 2010) as well as neuropeptide F (NPF), which is a fly ortholog of mammalian neuropeptide Y (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Keene et al., 2010 and Chung et al., 2017.

claim: Starvation promotes arousal in a manner dependent on neuropeptide F (NPF), which is a fly ortholog of mammalian neuropeptide Y.
source: Starvation promotes arousal in a manner dependent on the circadian clock genes Clock and cycle (Keene et al., 2010) as well as neuropeptide F (NPF), which is a fly ortholog of mammalian neuropeptide Y (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claim: Protein is one of the nutrients that contribute to the postprandial sleep drive in Drosophila.
source: On the other hand, protein is one of the nutrients that contribute to the postprandial sleep drive in Drosophila (Murphy et al., 2016) and this observation is possibly relevant to SPET.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Murphy et al., 2016.

claim: Leucokinin (Lk) and Lk receptor (Lkr) play important roles in dietary protein-induced postprandial sleep.
source: While Leucokinin (Lk) and Lk receptor (Lkr) play important roles in dietary protein-induced postprandial sleep (Murphy et al., 2016) and in starvation-induced arousal (Murakami et al., 2016), we observed comparable SPET between hypomorphic mutants of Lk or Lkr and their heterozygous controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murphy et al., 2016 and Murakami et al., 2016.

claim: Leucokinin (Lk) and Lk receptor (Lkr) play important roles in starvation-induced arousal.
source: While Leucokinin (Lk) and Lk receptor (Lkr) play important roles in dietary protein-induced postprandial sleep (Murphy et al., 2016) and in starvation-induced arousal (Murakami et al., 2016), we observed comparable SPET between hypomorphic mutants of Lk or Lkr and their heterozygous controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Murakami et al., 2016.

claim: Comparable SPET was observed between hypomorphic mutants of Lk or Lkr and their heterozygous controls.
source: While Leucokinin (Lk) and Lk receptor (Lkr) play important roles in dietary protein-induced postprandial sleep (Murphy et al., 2016) and in starvation-induced arousal (Murakami et al., 2016), we observed comparable SPET between hypomorphic mutants of Lk or Lkr and their heterozygous controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing comparable SPET in Lk or Lkr mutants, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: SPET and its neural basis reveal a sleep-regulatory mechanism distinct from those involved in sleep plasticity relevant to food intake.
source: Therefore, SPET and its neural basis reveal a sleep-regulatory mechanism distinct from those involved in sleep plasticity relevant to food intake.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that SPET is independent of Lk/Lkr signaling.

claim: Alpha-ketobutyrate, GABA, and the ketone body beta-hydroxybutyrate act as competitive substrates in common enzymatic reactions.
source: It has been previously shown that alpha-ketobutyrate, GABA, and the ketone body beta-hydroxybutyrate act as competitive substrates in common enzymatic reactions (Beyerinck and Brass, 1987; Lund et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beyerinck and Brass, 1987; Lund et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2009.

claim: Functional interactions of beta-hydroxybutyrate or gamma-hydroxybutyrate with GABAergic signaling have been well documented.
source: Moreover, functional interactions of beta-hydroxybutyrate or gamma-hydroxybutyrate with GABAergic signaling have been well documented (Absalom et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2009; Carter et al., 2005; Lund et al., 2011; Nasrallah et al., 2010; Snead and Gibson, 2005; Suzuki et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Absalom et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2009; Carter et al., 2005; Lund et al., 2011; Nasrallah et al., 2010; Snead and Gibson, 2005; Suzuki et al., 2009.

claim: Threonine and GABA derivatives have anti-convulsive effects.
source: Finally, threonine and GABA derivatives have anti-convulsive effects (Growdon et al., 1991; Hauser et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1990), which further support their common structural and functional relevance to GABAergic signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Growdon et al., 1991; Hauser et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1990.

claim: The removal of the amino group is the initial step for amino acid metabolism, and various transaminases mediate its transfer between amino acids and alpha-keto acids.
source: The removal of the amino group is the initial step for amino acid metabolism, and various transaminases mediate its transfer between amino acids and alpha-keto acids.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in biochemistry.

claim: A group of amino acids (i.e., glutamate, glycine, serine, and threonine) has their own deaminases that can selectively remove the amino group.
source: On the other hand, a group of amino acids (i.e., glutamate, glycine, serine, and threonine) has their own deaminases that can selectively remove the amino group (Bender, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bender, 2014.

claim: The presence of specific deaminases is indicative of active mechanisms that individually fine-tune the baseline levels of these amino acids in metabolism, and possibly in the context of other physiological processes as well.
source: The presence of these specific deaminases is indicative of active mechanisms that individually fine-tune the baseline levels of these amino acids in metabolism, and possibly in the context of other physiological processes as well.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the existence of specific deaminases.

claim: Glutamate, glycine, and serine have conserved roles as neurotransmitters or neuromodulators important for brain function, including sleep regulation.
source: This idea is further supported by the conserved roles of glutamate, glycine, and serine as neurotransmitters or neuromodulators important for brain function, including sleep regulation (Kawai et al., 2015; Tomita et al., 2017; Zimmerman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kawai et al., 2015; Tomita et al., 2017; Zimmerman et al., 2017.

claim: Serine, glycine, and threonine constitute a common metabolic pathway.
source: In fact, serine, glycine, and threonine constitute a common metabolic pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and threonine may contribute indirectly to glycine- or serine-dependent activation of sleep-promoting NMDAR (Kawai et al., 2015; Tomita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on established biochemical knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Threonine may contribute indirectly to glycine- or serine-dependent activation of sleep-promoting NMDAR.
source: In fact, serine, glycine, and threonine constitute a common metabolic pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and threonine may contribute indirectly to glycine- or serine-dependent activation of sleep-promoting NMDAR (Kawai et al., 2015; Tomita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to Kawai et al., 2015; Tomita et al., 2015.

claim: Sleep-modulatory effects of dietary glycine were distinct from SPET.
source: Nonetheless, we found that sleep-modulatory effects of dietary glycine were distinct from SPET and thus, we speculate that threonine may act as an independent neuromodulator, similar to other amino acids with their dedicated deaminases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing different effects of glycine and threonine on sleep.

claim: Threonine may act as an independent neuromodulator, similar to other amino acids with their dedicated deaminases.
source: Nonetheless, we found that sleep-modulatory effects of dietary glycine were distinct from SPET and thus, we speculate that threonine may act as an independent neuromodulator, similar to other amino acids with their dedicated deaminases.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental data and the existence of threonine-specific deaminase.

claim: The metabolic pathway of serine-glycine-threonine functions as a key sleep-regulatory module in response to metabolic sleep cues (e.g., food ingredients and dietary stress).
source: These two pieces of our relevant works establish a compelling model that the metabolic pathway of serine-glycine-threonine functions as a key sleep-regulatory module in response to metabolic sleep cues (e.g., food ingredients and dietary stress).
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective evidence from the current study and prior work on serine.
